why: The statement is only the Millennium problem's title. Clay's formulation awards the prize for establishing any one of alternatives A–D, so proving forced breakdown (C, or D) answers the problem as Clay poses it; it is not one part of a conjunction. On that reading I scored OpenAI's forced blow-up claim `whole`. It is `unreviewed`: the Lean build is not a reading (F7), and the named engagements are critiques, a kernel replay and conditional results, not verifications. It is `doubtful` rather than knocked down, because the Bastounis et al. mismatches are specific but are fidelity gaps that nobody has shown break the theorem. By OpenAI's own quote its model produced the proof, so `generated`. Blow-up contradicts smoothness, so I gave the event direction `refuted` with a counterexample object. The unforced regularity claims (Ri ×2, Polozov, Paseva, Nwankpa, Academia) would each also answer the problem in full, but each carries several F10 signals together and is set aside as `not_credible`. Neighbouring equations, hypodissipation, non-uniqueness, shell models, numerics and the computability family are `variant` or `none`. The Buckmaster–Alpöge and IPM events record no ai.systems entry with a quote, so they are `none`.
doubts: Close call on scope: if the statement is read as the classical unforced regularity question (A/B), the OpenAI event is a `variant` (forced) rather than `whole`. On the direction, Clay's C/D are existence questions, so the blow-up object could equally be called a witness for C; I chose counterexample because the title asserts existence and smoothness. Ri 2026 (22 Jan 2026) falls before the snapshot although the record's flag says otherwise. Scientific American reports three unnamed withdrawals from OpenAI's 6 Oct release; whether the Navier–Stokes manuscript is among them is not established. The OpenAI AI quote comes from a search snippet of an unopened page, though Quanta and Wikipedia corroborate it.
